title: SaTPO: Text-to-Image Safety Alignment via Transition Preference Optimization

paper.title: SaTPO: Text-to-Image Safety Alignment via Transition Preference Optimization
paper.abstract:
Abstract Safety alignment of text-to-image diffusion models aims to suppress harmful content without compromising useful generation capabilities. However, preferences over completed images compress multidimensional generation factors into a coarse signal, potentially driving changes beyond those required for safety.
To address this, we propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO), which enforces step-wise alignment during denoising. SaTPO leverages the insight that an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form a tightly coupled preference pair when conditioned on a shared parent state and noise realization.
By anchoring optimization on identical parent states, SaTPO eliminates historical trajectory divergence, confining safety adaptation to an incremental alignment while preserving task-relevant semantics.
Multi-scale drift constraints and benign replay further limit behavioral deviation and preserve ordinary generation.
We additionally construct CoProPV, a refined dataset ensuring visually verified contrasts.
Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate improved safety-quality trade-offs.
Compared with AlignGuard, PerspectiveVision unsafe-detection rates on Inappropriate Image Prompts decrease from 12.70% to 6.00% and from 15.04% to 9.30%, respectively, while FID improves from 32.28 to 25.95 and from 36.50 to 27.51. Warning: this paper includes potentially offensive content.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image diffusion models have become powerful tools for visual content creation, producing diverse and realistic images from natural language descriptions ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) . These capabilities also introduce risks, as the models can generate sexually explicit, violent, or otherwise harmful content in response to user prompts ( Qu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Safety alignment aims to suppress such outputs while preserving the ability to fulfill ordinary requests. Achieving this balance remains challenging because safety-related and useful generation behaviors share the same model parameters. While early efforts focused on prompt filtering, sampling guidance, or concept editing ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , recent advances leverage preference-based optimization to directly learn safe behaviors from paired supervision ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . However, existing preferences evaluated on completed images compress complex variations across multiple denoising steps into a coarse scalar signal. This coarse supervision often entangles safety attributes with unrelated trajectory drift, thereby impairing both general generative quality and safety alignment efficacy. Figure 1: Preference construction for diffusion alignment. AlignGuard uses forward-noised completed-image pairs. LPO ranks step-level latent candidates with an external reward model. SaTPO couples one-step transitions from an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite using a shared parent state and noise. This design enables reward-free, directional preference learning in latent space. Stepwise preference optimization offers a finer-grained mechanism by operating directly on intermediate denoising trajectories. While pioneering step-level methods like LPO have been explored for general quality or aesthetic alignment ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , they heavily rely on a noise-aware latent reward model to score and rank intermediate candidate latents. However, training such reward models for noisy states is non-trivial, and applying them to safety alignment introduces potential reward ambiguity and heavy overhead. In this work, we observe that safety alignment possesses a unique structural advantage over aesthetic tuning: an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form an intrinsic, perfectly coupled preference pair without requiring any external reward model. As illustrated in Figure 1 , we use these prompts to generate one-step alternatives from the same parent state with shared Gaussian noise, making their difference exactly the rewrite-induced change in the transition mean. Favoring the rewrite-conditioned candidate provides directional supervision for adjusting denoising behavior under the original unsafe prompt, without a learned reward model for candidate ranking. We propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO) , a reward-free framework that aligns denoising trajectories through coupled one-step transition preferences. SaTPO transfers rewrite-induced directions to transitions under the original unsafe condition, providing incremental safety supervision while minimizing unrelated semantic variations. Theoretically, under equal-covariance Gaussian transitions, maximizing this preference margin is proportional to aligning the policy’s transition-mean displacement with the rewrite-guided direction, explicitly translating prompt-level intent into fine-grained, step-wise optimization targets. Directional supervision alone does not prevent unwanted behavioral changes: improving a relative preference margin can still degrade the preferred output ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . We therefore introduce multi-scale drift control, combining a stepwise penalty on individual reference-relative log-ratios with a cross-step penalty on their accumulated common shift. Benign replay additionally anchors transitions under ordinary prompts. Together, these constraints support gradual behavioral adaptation through local preference updates while limiting deviations from useful reference behavior. Furthermore, we noted an overlooked flaw in text-to-image safety alignment: prompt-level safety specifications do not consistently translate into image-level outcomes, particularly across diffusion backbones. To this end, we construct CoProPV , a visually verified refinement of CoProV2 ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . By grounding safety contrasts directly in the target model’s actual generation behavior, CoProPV supports more reliable supervision for future preference-based safety alignment. Extensive experiments across Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate that SaTPO significantly improves broad-safety detection rates and FID over strong baselines like AlignGuard, while exhibiting robust resistance to transferred adversarial attacks. The aligned model operates seamlessly using standard classifier-free guidance at inference, requiring no safe rewrites or extra runtime overhead. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose SaTPO, a safety alignment framework that converts prompt-level safety counterfactuals into coupled transition preferences at a shared state and noise, providing explicit directional supervision without learned reward-model ranking. • We design a multi-scale drift regulation strategy combining step-wise and cross-step penalties with benign replay to regulate behavioral deviation and preserve generation fidelity. • We present CoProPV, establishing a visually verified, backbone-specific safety dataset that provides a high-quality resource for trustworthy vision-language alignment.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Safe Text-to-Image Generation. Safety defenses operate externally around the generator or internally within it ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . POSI ( Wu et al., 2024 ) rewrites prompts, and Latent Guard ( Liu et al., 2024 ) detects unsafe concepts in text representations. Safe Latent Diffusion ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) applies denoising-time safety guidance; SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) combines text-subspace projection with latent re-attention. Internal defenses include negative-guidance distillation in ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , closed-form cross-attention updates in UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , scalable erasure in MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , and iterative target-embedding erasure in RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) . Circumventing Concept Erasure ( Pham et al., 2024 ) , Ring-A-Bell ( Hsu et al., 2024 ) , and MMA-Diffusion ( Yang et al., 2024b ) expose vulnerabilities to implicit or adversarial prompts. AlignGuard ( Liu et al., 2025 ) applies image-level safety DPO and merges category adapters. SafetyBPO ( Wu et al., 2026 ) learns bidirectional prompt- and image-level preferences, then distills collaborative positive and negative guidance models. Preference Optimization for Diffusion Models. DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) converts KL-regularized reward maximization into pairwise classification relative to a reference model. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) optimizes terminal rewards with policy gradients, while DPOK ( Fan et al., 2023 ) constrains distributional drift from the pretrained model. Diffusion-DPO ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) uses a diffusion likelihood bound. DSPO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) distills a preferred distribution’s score function, and Direct Distributional Optimization ( Kawata et al., 2025 ) optimizes a reference-regularized distribution. Diffusion-NPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) trains a negative-preference CFG branch. Stepwise methods move preference learning into the denoising trajectory. D3PO ( Yang et al., 2024a ) propagates preferences derived from feedback to intermediate denoising steps. SPO ( Liang et al., 2025 ) ranks shared-state candidates with a step-aware model, and LPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) learns rewards in noisy latent space. RDPO ( Wu et al., 2025 ) corrects intermediate-reward bias. Diffusion-SDPO ( Fu et al., 2026 ) addresses winner–loser update imbalance. Building on stepwise comparisons, SaTPO constructs one-step preferences from an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite using a shared parent state and noise, without reward-model ranking.

sections.heading: 4 Safety Transition Preference Optimization
sections.text: Given an unsafe prompt c U c^{U} and its safe rewrite c S c^{S} , we propose SaTPO to translate prompt safety counterfactuals into step-level preference supervision. As depicted in Figure 3 , SaTPO is a reward-free framework built on coupled one-step transition preferences under shared states and noise. Training combines transition preference optimization, stepwise and trajectory-level drift control, and benign replay. Algorithm 1 in Appendix B.1 gives the procedure.

sections.heading: 4.1 Backbone-specific safety Pair Construction
sections.text: We construct the backbone-specific CoProPV dataset to address potential mismatches between prompt-level and generated-image safety labels. Specifically, we regenerate images for all 10,983 CoProV2 training pairs of unsafe prompts and safe rewrites ( c U , c S ) (c^{U},c^{S}) using fixed seeds on SD-v1.5 and SDXL. Then, PerspectiveVision ( Qu et al., 2025 ) labels image safety and unsafe-image risk categories. Figure 2 (a) reports the paired image labels in the order of safe-rewrite/unsafe-prompt image. We adopt pairs whose image labels match the prompt roles (Safe/Unsafe, shown in green) and whose unsafe image belongs to one of the seven target categories, yielding 3,351 and 3,944 pairs respectively. Figure 2: CoProPV label distribution and preference-gap attenuation along denoising trajectories. (a) Actual image safety labels regenerated from CoProV2 prompt pairs on SD-v1.5 and SDXL. (b) Evolution of the mean SafetyLRM score difference ( preferred − rejected \text{preferred}-\text{rejected} ) across denoising timesteps for SDXL child latents. As denoising progresses ( t → 0 t\to 0 ), the preference gap diminishes, providing empirical support for SaTPO’s progressive trajectory regularization.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Figure 4: Selected qualitative comparisons across seven risk categories on SD-v1.5 and SDXL. Methods share prompts and random seeds within each backbone. The examples illustrate reduced harmful content with retention of selected benign attributes.

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Backbones and Training. We train Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD-v1.5) and SDXL Base ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) on their respective CoProPV subsets, using LoRA ranks of 8 and 64. SD-v1.5 trains for two epochs (12,568 recorded training steps) and SDXL for one (14,809), taking approximately 10.11 and 77 hours on a single NVIDIA A800 GPU. We use AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , 20-step stochastic DDIM ( Song et al., 2021 ) candidate generation, and CFG 7.5. Appendix B.2 provides the full configurations and training-time comparison. Evaluation. Safety evaluation uses 5,000 prompt–seed evaluations from I2P ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , all 934 unsafe prompts in Unsafe Diffusion (UD) ( Qu et al., 2023 ) , and 1,000 prompts sampled from NSFW-56k ( Li et al., 2024 ) . Benign-quality evaluation uses the 5,000 MS COCO val2017 images and selected captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . Methods share prompts and initial noise within each backbone. SD-v1.5 uses 512 2 512^{2} images and 50-step DDIM; SDXL uses 1024 2 1024^{2} images and 20-step Euler sampling. Both use CFG 7.5 with the output safety checker disabled. Appendix C provides further details. Baselines and LPO Safety Adaptation. We compare SaTPO with the original public SD-v1.5 and SDXL models (Base) and existing safeguards, including the Medium and Max variants of SLD ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) , ESD-u ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) , and the image-level safety-preference methods AlignGuard ( Liu et al., 2025 ) and SafetyBPO ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . We use the official AlignGuard and SafetyBPO weights. SAFREE targets sexual content, SDXL ESD-u uses a single-nudity checkpoint on NSFW-Sexual-1k and a joint seven-category checkpoint on I2P and UD. Appendix C.2 details the baseline configurations. On CoProPV, we adapt LPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) to rank four unsafe-prompt candidates per step with SafetyLRM, retaining the official threshold filtering and clipped DPO. We report SDXL results in the main comparison, SD-v1.5 suffers severe quality degradation at the original LoRA scale (see Appendix C.8 ). Metrics. We report detection rates (%, ↓ \downarrow ) from seven-category PerspectiveVision (PV) ( Qu et al., 2025 ) , Q16 ( Schramowski et al., 2022 ) , and NudeNet ( Bedapudi, 2023 ) (genital exposure). Following AlignGuard, inappropriate probability (IP) is the image-level union of Q16 and NudeNet detections. Benign metrics are CLIP text–image similarity ( ↑ \uparrow ) ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID, ↓ \downarrow ) relative to real COCO images ( Heusel et al., 2017 ; Parmar et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: 5.2 Main results
sections.text: Safety Comparisons. As shown in Table 1 , SaTPO achieves the lowest PV, Q16, and IP detection rates on I2P and UD for both backbones. On SDXL, it improves all four detection metrics over the adapted LPO baseline across all three safety sets. Gains extend to Q16 and IP, which are unused for data qualification, and to PV across all seven SDXL prompt categories, as shown in Table 3 . Appendices C.4 and C.5 provide category and exposure-type results. Qualitative Comparisons. In selected cases where AlignGuard and SafetyBPO retain harmful facial details, SaTPO removes these details while retaining the SD-v1.5 portrait subjects, as shown in Figure 4 . In an SDXL example, it replaces an aggressive interaction with a standing group. Appendix C.7 provides further comparisons. Benign Generation. As shown in Figure 5 (b), SaTPO has lower COCO FID than AlignGuard on both backbones and SafetyBPO on SD-v1.5. Base has the highest CLIP similarity and lowest FID. SDXL LPO has higher CLIP similarity but worse FID than SaTPO (see Appendix C.8 ). Figure 5 (a) shows preservation of the pitching action and bear appearance altered by AlignGuard. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: SaTPO learns safety preferences over one-step transitions coupled through shared parent states and noise, with backbone-specific CoProPV qualification, drift control, and benign replay. On SD-v1.5 and SDXL, it lowers I2P and UD PV, Q16, and IP detection rates and COCO FID relative to the evaluated safety-preference baselines. Safety gains also extend to fixed adversarial prompts. Ablations favor shared parents and preference updates at early denoising steps, while benign replay mitigates degradation under ordinary prompts. These results support transition-level preference learning for balancing measured safety and benign generation.

sections.heading: C.8 LPO safety adaptation
sections.text: SafetyLRM adapts LPO’s noise-aware latent reward architecture ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) to safety preferences. Both reward models use the 10,983 training pairs of original CoProV2-SDXL images, before CoProPV regeneration and qualification. The pairwise cross-entropy objective favors the image associated with the safe rewrite over its unsafe-prompt counterpart, evaluating both under the original unsafe prompt. Each pair uses a shared timestep sampled from { 1 , 51 , … , 951 } \{1,51,\ldots,951\} and independent noise for its two images. We train the corresponding SDXL and SD-v1.5 architectures for 30,000 updates with batch size 1, Adafactor, learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} , and weight decay 0.01, at resolutions 1024 2 1024^{2} and 512 2 512^{2} , respectively. Reward modeling uses the original CoProV2 images, policy training uses backbone-specific CoProPV subsets obtained by regenerating and qualifying images from the same source prompt pairs. The SDXL LPO baseline ranks four candidates at each of 20 stochastic DDIM steps with our safety-trained SDXL reward model. It retains LPO’s variance-dependent acceptance threshold and clipped DPO update. Training uses the 3,944 CoProPV prompt pairs, one epoch, LoRA rank 64, CFG 7.5, β = 500 \beta=500 , clipping ε = 0.1 \varepsilon=0.1 , and learning rate 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The threshold ranges from 0.45 to 0.60. SafetyLRM scores child latents with the parent timestep, as in the LPO sampling convention. Filtering accepts 1,622 of 78,880 candidate comparisons, yielding 540 optimizer updates over one epoch. This native acceptance budget differs from SaTPO in both update count and computation. On COCO-5000, SDXL LPO obtains CLIP 0.2686 and FID 28.08. Relative to SaTPO’s 0.2602 and 27.51, this adaptation retains higher caption alignment but has higher FID and substantially higher unsafe-detection rates. For SD-v1.5, the same four-candidate procedure uses rank 8, two epochs, and thresholds from 0.35 to 0.50. The trained policy at LoRA scale 1.0 exhibits severe quality degradation, with COCO CLIP 0.1653 and FID 207.57 (Table 13 ). The low PV rate accompanies degraded generation. However, preferences over completed images compress multidimensional generation factors into a coarse signal, potentially driving changes beyond those required for safety. To address this, we propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO), which enforces step-wise alignment during denoising. SaTPO leverages the insight that an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form a tightly coupled preference pair when conditioned on a shared parent state and noise realization. By anchoring optimization on identical parent states, SaTPO eliminates historical trajectory divergence, confining safety adaptation to an incremental alignment while preserving task-relevant semantics. Multi-scale drift constraints and benign replay further limit behavioral deviation and preserve ordinary generation. We additionally construct CoProPV, a refined dataset ensuring visually verified contrasts. Experiments on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate improved safety-quality trade-offs. Compared with AlignGuard, PerspectiveVision unsafe-detection rates on Inappropriate Image Prompts decrease from 12.70% to 6.00% and from 15.04% to 9.30%, respectively, while FID improves from 32.28 to 25.95 and from 36.50 to 27.51. Warning: this paper includes potentially offensive content. 1 Introduction Text-to-image diffusion models have become powerful tools for visual content creation, producing diverse and realistic images from natural language descriptions ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) . These capabilities also introduce risks, as the models can generate sexually explicit, violent, or otherwise harmful content in response to user prompts ( Qu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Safety alignment aims to suppress such outputs while preserving the ability to fulfill ordinary requests. Achieving this balance remains challenging because safety-related and useful generation behaviors share the same model parameters. While early efforts focused on prompt filtering, sampling guidance, or concept editing ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Schramowski et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , recent advances leverage preference-based optimization to directly learn safe behaviors from paired supervision ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Wallace et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . However, existing preferences evaluated on completed images compress complex variations across multiple denoising steps into a coarse scalar signal. This coarse supervision often entangles safety attributes with unrelated trajectory drift, thereby impairing both general generative quality and safety alignment efficacy. Figure 1: Preference construction for diffusion alignment. AlignGuard uses forward-noised completed-image pairs. LPO ranks step-level latent candidates with an external reward model. SaTPO couples one-step transitions from an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite using a shared parent state and noise. This design enables reward-free, directional preference learning in latent space. Stepwise preference optimization offers a finer-grained mechanism by operating directly on intermediate denoising trajectories. While pioneering step-level methods like LPO have been explored for general quality or aesthetic alignment ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , they heavily rely on a noise-aware latent reward model to score and rank intermediate candidate latents. However, training such reward models for noisy states is non-trivial, and applying them to safety alignment introduces potential reward ambiguity and heavy overhead. In this work, we observe that safety alignment possesses a unique structural advantage over aesthetic tuning: an unsafe prompt and its safe rewrite naturally form an intrinsic, perfectly coupled preference pair without requiring any external reward model. As illustrated in Figure 1 , we use these prompts to generate one-step alternatives from the same parent state with shared Gaussian noise, making their difference exactly the rewrite-induced change in the transition mean. Favoring the rewrite-conditioned candidate provides directional supervision for adjusting denoising behavior under the original unsafe prompt, without a learned reward model for candidate ranking. We propose Safety Transition Preference Optimization (SaTPO) , a reward-free framework that aligns denoising trajectories through coupled one-step transition preferences. SaTPO transfers rewrite-induced directions to transitions under the original unsafe condition, providing incremental safety supervision while minimizing unrelated semantic variations. Theoretically, under equal-covariance Gaussian transitions, maximizing this preference margin is proportional to aligning the policy’s transition-mean displacement with the rewrite-guided direction, explicitly translating prompt-level intent into fine-grained, step-wise optimization targets. Directional supervision alone does not prevent unwanted behavioral changes: improving a relative preference margin can still degrade the preferred output ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . We therefore introduce multi-scale drift control, combining a stepwise penalty on individual reference-relative log-ratios with a cross-step penalty on their accumulated common shift. Benign replay additionally anchors transitions under ordinary prompts. Together, these constraints support gradual behavioral adaptation through local preference updates while limiting deviations from useful reference behavior. Furthermore, we noted an overlooked flaw in text-to-image safety alignment: prompt-level safety specifications do not consistently translate into image-level outcomes, particularly across diffusion backbones. To this end, we construct CoProPV , a visually verified refinement of CoProV2 ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . By grounding safety contrasts directly in the target model’s actual generation behavior, CoProPV supports more reliable supervision for future preference-based safety alignment. Extensive experiments across Stable Diffusion v1.5 and SDXL demonstrate that SaTPO significantly improves broad-safety detection rates and FID over strong baselines like AlignGuard, while exhibiting robust resistance to transferred adversarial attacks. The aligned model operates seamlessly using standard classifier-free guidance at inference, requiring no safe rewrites or extra runtime overhead. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose SaTPO, a safety alignment framework that converts prompt-level safety counterfactuals into coupled transition preferences at a shared state and noise, providing explicit directional supervision without learned reward-model ranking. • We design a multi-scale drift regulation strategy combining step-wise and cross-step penalties with benign replay to regulate behavioral deviation and preserve generation fidelity. • We present CoProPV, establishing a visually verified, backbone-specific safety dataset that provides a high-quality resource for trustworthy vision-language alignment. 2 Related Work Safe Text-to-Image Generation. Safety defenses operate externally around the generator or internally within it ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) . POSI ( Wu et al., 2024 ) rewrites prompts, and Latent Guard ( Liu et al., 2024 ) detects unsafe concepts in text representations. Safe Latent Diffusion ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) applies denoising-time safety guidance; SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) combines text-subspace projection with latent re-attention. Internal defenses include negative-guidance distillation in ESD ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , closed-form cross-attention updates in UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , scalable erasure in MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , and iterative target-embedding erasure in RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) . Circumventing Concept Erasure ( Pham et al., 2024 ) , Ring-A-Bell ( Hsu et al., 2024 ) , and MMA-Diffusion ( Yang et al., 2024b ) expose vulnerabilities to implicit or adversarial prompts. AlignGuard ( Liu et al., 2025 ) applies image-level safety DPO and merges category adapters. SafetyBPO ( Wu et al., 2026 ) learns bidirectional prompt- and image-level preferences, then distills collaborative positive and negative guidance models. Preference Optimization for Diffusion Models. DPO ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) converts KL-regularized reward maximization into pairwise classification relative to a reference model. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) optimizes terminal rewards with policy gradients, while DPOK ( Fan et al., 2023 ) constrains distributional drift from the pretrained model. Diffusion-DPO ( Wallace et al., 2024 ) uses a diffusion likelihood bound. DSPO ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) distills a preferred distribution’s score function, and Direct Distributional Optimization ( Kawata et al., 2025 ) optimizes a reference-regularized distribution. Diffusion-NPO ( Wang et al., 2025 ) trains a negative-preference CFG branch. Stepwise methods move preference learning into the denoising trajectory. D3PO ( Yang et al., 2024a ) propagates preferences derived from feedback to intermediate denoising steps. SPO ( Liang et al., 2025 ) ranks shared-state candidates with a step-aware model, and LPO ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) learns rewards in noisy latent space. RDPO ( Wu et al., 2025 ) corrects intermediate-reward bias. Diffusion-SDPO ( Fu et al., 2026 ) addresses winner–loser update imbalance. We train Stable Diffusion v1.5 (SD-v1.5) and SDXL Base ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) on their respective CoProPV subsets, using LoRA ranks of 8 and 64. SD-v1.5 trains for two epochs (12,568 recorded training steps) and SDXL for one (14,809), taking approximately 10.11 and 77 hours on a single NVIDIA A800 GPU. Benign-quality evaluation uses the 5,000 MS COCO val2017 images and selected captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . Methods share prompts and initial noise within each backbone.
